clinicalPearls: Classically a triad of recurrent orofacial oedema, recurrent (often alternating) peripheral facial nerve palsy, and a fissured (scrotal/plicated) tongue, though the complete triad is uncommon
Most patients present with only one or two features, and the lip swelling (granulomatous cheilitis of Miescher) is frequently the first and most persistent sign
Facial swelling is typically non-pitting, painless, and initially transient but tends to become firm and permanent with recurrent attacks
Lip biopsy may show non-caseating granulomas, but a normal histology does not exclude the diagnosis
The condition sits within the spectrum of orofacial granulomatosis and can overlap with Crohn disease and sarcoidosis, which should be considered particularly in younger patients
Facial palsy may precede, accompany, or follow the swelling and can be recurrent, mimicking repeated Bell palsy
Management is largely supportive and anti-inflammatory (intralesional or systemic corticosteroids); refractory persistent lip swelling may be reduced with reduction cheiloplasty
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome is characterised by non-caseating granulomatous inflammation affecting the orofacial soft tissues, with lymphoedema and perivascular granulomas obstructing lymphatic drainage and producing recurrent, eventually persistent, oedema. The facial nerve is thought to be compromised by granulomatous or oedematous swelling within its bony canal, producing lower motor neurone palsy that may recur. The underlying trigger is unclear but is presumed to be an aberrant delayed-type immune response, possibly to dietary, dental, or microbial antigens, and the disorder overlaps mechanistically with other granulomatous conditions such as Crohn disease and sarcoidosis. The fissured tongue is regarded as a developmental/constitutional feature associated with the syndrome rather than a granulomatous lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Orofacial granulomatosis secondary to Crohn disease
additionalInvestigations: Labial or oral mucosal biopsy seeking non-caseating granulomas
Faecal calprotectin, and gastrointestinal endoscopy where Crohn disease is suspected
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and chest imaging to screen for sarcoidosis
Patch testing and dietary/allergen assessment for contactants such as cinnamon and benzoates
C1 esterase inhibitor level and complement studies to exclude hereditary angio-oedema
MRI of the facial nerve if palsy is atypical or fails to recover
redFlags: Systemic features (weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, respiratory symptoms) suggesting Crohn disease or sarcoidosis
Progressive or incomplete recovery of facial palsy raising concern for a compressive or neoplastic lesion
Rapidly evolving airway or tongue swelling suggesting angio-oedema rather than granulomatous oedema
Unilateral fixed mass rather than diffuse recurrent swelling
reference.prognosis: The course is chronic and relapsing; early oedema is transient but repeated attacks can lead to permanent disfiguring lip swelling. Facial palsy often recovers but may be incomplete after recurrent episodes. The syndrome itself is benign, though associated systemic granulomatous disease influences the overall outlook.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing recurrent orofacial oedema as allergic angio-oedema and treating only with antihistamines
Assuming a normal lip biopsy excludes the diagnosis, since granulomas are patchy
Overlooking underlying Crohn disease or sarcoidosis, especially in children and young adults
Treating recurrent facial palsy as simple Bell palsy without recognising the wider syndrome
Attributing the fissured tongue to poor hygiene rather than a syndromic feature
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Reduce the granulomatous orofacial swelling with corticosteroids given intralesionally or systemically
Use steroid-sparing immunomodulators such as clofazimine, methotrexate or a TNF-alpha inhibitor for persistent or refractory disease
Investigate for and treat overlapping Crohn disease and sarcoidosis within the orofacial granulomatosis spectrum
Undertake dietary exclusion and avoidance of implicated contactants such as cinnamon and benzoates identified on patch testing
Provide supportive facial-palsy care with eye protection, and consider reduction cheiloplasty or facial-nerve decompression for disfiguring persistent swelling
Coordinate multidisciplinary oral medicine, neurology, gastroenterology and dermatology input
